title: Dedication of Merit
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the dedication of merit on page one of the chant book, beginning with the old idea of merit and the story of Punika in The Hidden Lamp, who tells a Brahman that a cold river bath cannot wash away evil acts. Heigaku reads Bodhidharma on karma as cause and effect passing from one state of mind to the next, then Shantideva's verses of offering and dedication. Heigaku goes through the echo line by line, including the ten directions and the Lotus Sutra scene where Buddhas from every direction crowd in around the treasure stupa. The evening closes with the Prajnaparamita in three words: "Love this story."

sentences.text: Does everybody have a chant book?
We're in a series of talks where we started at the beginning of the chant book and we're working toward the end, and I think we're up to page one.
I'll be talking about the dedication of merit.

Buddhism evolved in the context of Hinduism, in the environment of Hinduism, which had this concept called merit: basically, action performed with virtue that leads toward ending the cycle of creation, of birth and death.
The old concept of merit had doing good, doing good works, as being virtuous and creating merit, good karma.
Chanting, performing religious activity, was considered virtuous and created good karma.
So by simply chanting, hey, we're able to be reborn as something better, something with less suffering, maybe eventually, after many, many lives, [unclear: "with none"].
There are some problems with that.
As an example of merit, I'm going to jump to *Hidden Lamp*, which we've talked about before, *Stories from Twenty-Five Centuries of Awakened Women*: the story of Punika, page 93.
*The slave Punika was a follower of the Buddha and attained the first stage of awakening while carrying water from the river to her master's house.
Sometime later, she was again bringing water from the river when she saw the Brahman Udakasurika taking a ritual bath.
She said to him, "I must come down to the river even on cold days like today because I am a water carrier and a slave.
But why do you come to the river even when it makes you shiver with the cold?
What are you afraid of?"
"You know the laws of karma," he said.
"I am washing away my past evil acts."*
So that understanding was that merit, by performing religious activities, we acquire merit and we move on in our spiritual journey.
*"Who told you that would work?" she asked.
"If this were true, frogs, turtles and water snakes would all go to heaven.
And evildoers like pork butchers, thieves and executioners could all be cleansed with just a bath.
Besides, doesn't water wash away your merit too?
It would be better to avoid doing evil in the first place.
So spare yourself from this freezing water and go home."
The Brahman saw the truth of her words and tried to give her his robe in gratitude, but she refused.
Instead, she suggested that he should take refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Sangha and train in the precepts.
He took refuge and said to her, "Your words have washed me clean."*
Along with merit comes this concept of karma.
We think of karma as some magical, ancient superstition, but it's really just cause and effect: doing good, good arises, and in the everyday harmful work that we do, that arises.
So you might think, well, I'm a modern, technological person, I don't believe in karma.
Basically what you're saying is, I don't believe in cause and effect.
Now, that's a valid philosophical position.
I just want you to understand that you're saying, I don't believe in cause and effect.
Bodhidharma, our first ancestor in China, has this to say about karma:
*Mortals keep creating karma and mistakenly insist that there's no retribution.
But can they deny suffering?
Can they deny that what the present state of mind sows, the next state of mind reaps?
How can they escape?*
It's interesting that oftentimes, even in the context of this school, when we talk about karma we think of long-term changes.
But Bodhidharma here is going right from this state of mind from now to now.
What there is in the first one affects the second one.
*If the present state of mind sows nothing, the next state of mind reaps nothing.
Don't misconceive karma.*
Did you know that at the Kansas City Marathon a few months ago, a Missouri professor broke a world record?
This was the world record for the longest scarf knitted by a person while running a marathon.
The previous record had been six feet, and he doubled it: he knitted a scarf 12 feet long running the marathon.
When we talk about breaking a record running a marathon, the mind immediately goes to breaking a running record.
And then we find out about the scarf, and it kind of tips everything on its head.

In just that way, in the early days of Buddhism, the good Buddhists and Hindus were busy doing their good works and practicing rigorously to achieve merit, when along come Mahayana teachings and say, oh, by the way, give away that merit too.

The Mahayana teachings recognized that this distinction of the self that I'm doing merit for really isn't different from other beings, and so we really can't be acting for our own benefit and not acting for the benefit of all beings.
Now, that's a bit of an oversimplification.
The Theravada practices did have dedication of merit, giving merit away to others.
It was seen in the context of: we give merit away to others because it cleanses our minds and allows us enlightenment.
We often think of Buddhism after the days of the Buddha as having gone to Tibet and then again gone to China, Cambodia, but it didn't leave India.
So in the year 700 there's an important teacher called Shantideva, one of Chris Burkhart's favorite teachers, with good reason.
Shantideva is able to really get at what we do.

Many of the teachings we study are difficult to penetrate, but Shantideva recognizes that we're sitting here, we're trying to do good and we fail, and we need support and we try again, and we need to keep trying, but we recognize that things go wrong.
In talking about giving tonight and the dedication of merit, a tool that Shantideva offers is offering beyond our means, basically giving what we don't have.
There was a gentle soul I was romantically involved with who didn't like receiving flowers because she didn't like having the flowers killed, cut.
That's good.
I could then give her flowers without cutting them: you know, this orchid is for you.
It's yours, and it can still live happily in the neighbor's garden, but it's dedicated to you.
So Shantideva goes on to giving.
Sorry, I have to go to the ebook for this.
We do have one in the library, but it's a translation that is fairly dry.
So, Shantideva on giving:
*To the Buddhas, those thus gone, and to the sacred Dharma, spotless and supremely rare, and to the Buddha's offspring, oceans of good qualities, that I might gain this precious attitude*
That's bodhicitta, by the way, the desire of awakening.
*I make a perfect offering.

I offer every fruit and flower, every kind of healing draft, and all the precious gems the world contains, with all pure waters of refreshment, every [unclear: "rot"] of precious jewels, all sweet and peaceful forest groves, the trees of paradise adorned with blossom, trees with branches bowed with perfect fruit, the perfumed fragrance of divine and other realms, all incense, wishing trees and trees of gems, all crops that grow without the tiller's care, and every sumptuous object worthy to be offered, lakes and meres adorned with lotuses, delightful with the sweet-voiced cries of water birds, and everything unclaimed and free, extending to the margins of the boundless sky.
I hold them all before my mind, and to the mighty sage, the greatest of our kind, and to their heirs, I make a perfect offering.
Sublime recipients, compassionate lords, oh think of me with love, accept these gifts of mine.
For destitute of merit, I am very poor.
I have no other wealth, and so, protectors, you whose wise intentions are for others' good, in your great power receive them for my sake.*
*Enlightened ones and all your bodhisattva heirs, I offer to you my body throughout all my lives.
Supreme courageous ones, accept me totally, for with devotion I will be your slave.*
Let me skip a bit.
So, knowing that the power of this teaching accepts us totally, he is giving all goodness to continue goodness.
*A bathing chamber excellently fragrant, with even floors of crystal, radiant and clear, and graceful pillars shimmering with gems, all hung about with gleaming canopies of pearls.
There the blissful Buddhas and their heirs I'll bathe with many a precious vase abrim with water fragrant and delightful, all to frequent strains of melody and song.
With cloths of unexampled quality, with spotless perfumed towels, I will dry them, and offer splendid scented clothes, well dyed and of surpassing excellence.
I will offer swelling clouds of frankincense whose ambient perfume ravishes the mind, and various foods and every kind of drink, all delicacies worthy of the gods.
I will offer lamps, precious lamps arranged in rows on lotuses of gold, a carpet of sweet flowers scattering upon the level, incense-sprinkled ground.

To those whose very nature is compassion, I will give vast palaces resounding with fair praise, all decked with precious pearls and beauteous pendant gems, gleaming jewels that deck the amplitude of space, fair and precious parasols adorned with golden shafts, all bordered round with hems of precious jewels, upright, well proportioned, pleasing to the eye.
Again, all this I give to all the Buddhas.
To shrines and all supports of bodhicitta, I bow down, to abbots who transmit the vows, to every learned master, and to all sublime practitioners of Dharma.*
Isn't that amazing, that that's possible, that we can give all that away?
It's recommended that we do so.
So dedication of merit is giving, a big step on the perfection of giving.

Remember the six perfections, the first one of which is dana paramita, the six paramitas: dana paramita, perfect giving, recognizing that the giver, receiver and the gift are all one, and that we are the giver and the receiver and the gift.
Back in *Hidden Lamp*, one of the commentaries, by Misha Shungen Merrill, is responding to the story of Punika.
*Five young story is everyone's story.
How do we sincerely practice the paramita, or perfection, of generosity without falling into dualistic thinking?
Our usual understanding of generosity is that there is one who gives things, material, time, energy, and one who receives them.
In the creation of giver and receiver, however, we are already lost in delusion, misunderstanding the fundamental nature of generosity: ending separation between self and other in giving.*
Of course our minds bring up that we are giving.
Of course there is the desire to get something out of giving.
And yet in recognizing it, and in recognizing how we are also the receiver, when we are also the receiver and the gift, we can start to let go of that.
One more thought on the dedication of merit from Shantideva before we actually look at the verse.
There is a dedication of merit in the services, in the chanting services we do.

In every chanting service we do, and we typically do the same one most nights here on Wednesday evening, but if you're present for a week-long session such as Samish, you may hear six or eight or more services over the course of the week, and all of them, after the chanting is done, have a part that's called the echo.
So the chanting has created this merit, supposedly.
Let me go with the Shantideva, where he starts, "Through these actions now performed."
In other words, I just did my chanting, I just did my religious practice.
*Through these actions now performed, and all the virtues I have gained, may the pain of every living being be wholly scattered and destroyed.
For all those ailing in the world, until their every sickness has been healed, may I myself become for them the doctor, nurse, the medicine itself.

Raining down a flood of food and drink, may I dispel the ills of thirst and famine, and in the eons marked by scarcity and want, may I myself appear as drink and sustenance for sentient beings poor and destitute.
May I become a treasure ever plentiful, and lie before them closely in their reach, a varied source of all that they might need.
My body thus, and all my goods besides, and all my merits gained and to be gained, I give them all and do not count the cost, to bring about the benefit of beings.*
*May I be a guard for those who are protectorless, a guide for those who journey on the road.
For those who wish to cross the water, may I be a boat, a raft, a bridge.
May I be an isle for those who yearn for land, a lamp for those who long for light.
For all who need a resting place, may I be a bed.
For those who need a servant, may I be their slave.
May I be the wishing jewel, the vase of wealth, a word of power and the supreme healing.
May I be the tree of miracles.
May I be for every being the abundant cow.
Just like the earth and space itself and all the other mighty elements, for boundless multitudes of beings may I always be the ground of life, the source of varied sustenance.
Thus for everything that lives, as far as the limits of the sky, may I be constantly their source of livelihood until they pass beyond all sorrow.*

*Just as all the Buddhas of the past have brought forth the awakened mind, and in the precepts of the bodhisattvas step by step abode and trained, likewise for the benefit of all beings I will bring to birth the awakened mind, and in those precepts step by step I will abide and train myself.*
Back to training.
We're giving this merit, but it's not merit that comes easily.
So we finish our chanting, and the Kokyo says, "May we awaken Buddhist compassion and luminous mirror wisdom."

So that echo starts with a prayer, may something happen, and then recounts the meritorious work that we just did: *With full awareness we have chanted the Great Wisdom Beyond Wisdom Sutra, the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom, the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyō for protecting life,* or whatever chants are in the service that was just done.
And then you hear, *We dedicate this merit.* Here it comes; the rest is basically a dedication of merit.

*Our original ancestor in India, great teacher Shakyamuni Buddha,* and on to the first woman ancestor, *Maha Prajapati, Bodhidharma, the women ancestors whose shining practice guides us to this day, the perfect wisdom bodhisattva Manjushri, and Avalokiteshvara.* And then we get to the part that is in the chant book.

However, there's an important line that's not in the chant book, and that is the line that the Kokyo sings: *Gratefully, we offer this virtue to all beings.* That's why the lines in the chant book are what they are:
*Gratefully, we offer the virtue to all beings.
All Buddhas, ten directions, three times.*
So, all Buddhas, ten directions.
The ten directions are north, south, east, west, northeast, southeast, northwest, southwest, up and down.
The three times are past, present and future.
When we say all Buddhas, traditionally Theravada emphasizes 28 Buddhas, listed in the Buddhavamsa.
But the Buddha has made clear that there are far more than just 28 named Buddhas.
How many Buddhas are there that we are dedicating this virtue to?
For that I'm going to go to the Lotus Sutra.
So during the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha's speaking and all of a sudden this stupa appears, this giant stupa hundreds of leagues long and high.
A league is the amount of distance that you can walk in about an hour, so you have to walk hundreds of hours to get from one end of this temple to the other.
According to tradition, the Buddha says:

*If someone wants me to show my body to the four groups, let the Buddhas who are embodiments of that Buddha and are preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions return together and assemble in one place.*
Nice.
So he's saying that the body of Buddha is all of these beings teaching in those ten directions.

*Then the Buddha emitted a beam of light from his tuft of white hair, immediately making visible all the Buddhas in five million billion myriads of lands to the east, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
They were filled with countless tens of millions of billions of bodhisattvas.

All the Buddhas in those lands preached various teachings with great, wonderful voices, and innumerable tens of millions of billions of bodhisattvas were also seen there, filling those lands and teaching the Dharma for the multitude.*
That's the east.
*It was the same in the southern, western and northern regions, and in the four intermediate directions, and up and down.

Wherever the beam of light shone from the tuft of white hair, then each of the Buddhas in the ten directions spoke to their multitudes of bodhisattvas, saying, "Good sons and daughters, now we have to go to Shakyamuni Buddha's world and make offerings to the treasure stupa."
Then those Buddhas arrived at this world and sat cross-legged.
Thus the three thousand great thousand-fold world was being filled, and those embodying Shakyamuni Buddha had not yet finished arriving from even one direction.*
So the entire universe was filled with buddhas, just from the east.
*Then Shakyamuni Buddha, wanting to make room for all the Buddhas, transformed two million billion myriads of lands in each of the eight directions, making them pure.*
What's more, he removed their human and heavenly beings to other lands.
So, in other words, to make room for all the Buddhas he had to clear away millions of billions of universes.
All right.
So: all Buddhas, ten directions, three times, all honored ones, bodhisattva mahasattvas.
A bodhisattva is an awakening being, a being who has vowed to put off enlightenment until we can all join hands together in enlightenment.
And a bodhisattva mahasattva is, you might consider, a high-ranking bodhisattva.
The Avatamsaka Sutra has a section describing bodhisattvas, listing ten attributes of bodhisattvas.
It's kind of like the Boy Scouts.
They are: joyful, stainless, luminous, radiant, difficult to conquer, present, far-going, immovable, with good thought, and a Dharma cloud.
Joyful, stainless, refulgent.
That is a word; I did not know it.
So about seven of those characteristics of a bodhisattva will make them a bodhisattva mahasattva.
Wisdom beyond wisdom, Maha Prajnaparamita.
Well, that should sound familiar to most of us, because we just spent the last six months studying the Prajnaparamita, teaching the great perfection of transcendent wisdom.
Conze was the translation that we studied some of, one of the greatest translators of the work, who studied it quite a bit, and I bring back again his summary of the Prajnaparamita.
He said:
*The thousands of lines of the Prajnaparamita can be summed up in the following two sentences.
One: one should become a bodhisattva, i.e., one who is content with nothing less than the all-knowledge attained through the perfection of wisdom for the sake of all beings.
And two: that there is no such thing as a bodhisattva, or as all-knowledge, or as a being, or as perfection of wisdom, or such thing as an attainment.
To accept both of these contradictory facts is to be perfect.*
There was another Conze quote that pretty much sums it up that I have misplaced, so maybe you'll encounter that someday.
You've heard of the Prajnaparamita in 8,000 lines, I think is the one that we studied.
There's a Prajnaparamita in 10,000 lines.
There's a Prajnaparamita in 100,000 lines.
And I would like to leave you this evening with the Prajnaparamita in three words.
This is a teaching that has been very powerful for me, a summary of the Prajnaparamita: Love this story.
First of all, it's a story.
We recognize that everything that arises when we're sitting on the cushion, or when we're driving our car, or meeting with people, it's a story.
It arises from components of this mind, and yet, recognizing it as a story, recognizing the fear when it arises, recognizing the pain as a story, we love it.
How do we love it?
Love's not a word we use a lot in Buddhist discussion.
We love by paying attention, by nurturing, by caring.
So it arises, we pay attention to it and care for it, and let's not leave out the word this: love this story, because this is all we have, this moment right now.
Love this story.
